metadata.title: Measuring different types and domains of AI knowledge: Developing and validating a performance-based scale

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used an online quota-sampled survey of adult internet users in Israel recruited via a polling service (October–November 2024). The analytic sample was restricted to participants who completed the survey, took at least 5 minutes, and passed three attention checks, yielding n=800. The manuscript does not report the use of complex survey weights (e.g., sampling/design weights) or any replicate-weight scheme; therefore, weighting cannot be confirmed from the provided text. Because the analyses are primarily psychometric/SEM/CFA and group comparisons rather than ML prediction, the paper’s weighting strategy is not documented in a way that would allow replication with survey-weighted estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are performance-based test scores and indices derived from a custom AI/GenAI knowledge inventory, plus Likert-scale attitudes and trust measures; the paper does not use ILSA-style PV achievement scaling. Missing-data handling is not reported in the provided text beyond excluding participants based on completion time and attention checks, so the specific treatment of item-level missingness (e.g., for indices requiring 3+ valid answers) is unclear. This is a reporting gap because the study computes several averaged indices and factor models that can be sensitive to how missing responses are handled.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Online survey via Qualtrics (Oct–Nov 2024) among adult internet users in Israel using quota sampling by gender, age, and education. From 1143 initial participants, the study excluded 55 who did not complete the survey, 55 who completed in under 5 minutes, and 233 who failed at least one of three attention checks, resulting in a final count of 800 participants. For some indices (attitudes toward AI; trust in GenAI), the paper reports averaging only for participants with three or more valid answers (attitudes: n=786; trust: n=781), implying additional validity-based inclusion for those constructs.

main_findings.dataset_used: Custom AI/GenAI knowledge inventory (Israel, Oct–Nov 2024 adult internet users)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Known-group tests: Overall score ANOVA F=47.24 (2, 794), p<.001, η2=.106 for GenAI experience; Age group F=26.02 (4, 361.2), p<.001, η2=.110; Education level F=26.02 (4, 361.2), p<.001, η2=.110; Gender t(796)=-3.180, p=.002. SEM fit indices (overall model): CFI=.819, TLI=.811, RMSEA=.06, SRMSR=.067. Factor associations within CPE/TUS: CPE inter-factor r=.621 to .825; TUS inter-factor r=.847 to .995 (p<.001). Additional analysis (Content AI knowledge score (0–9)): Known-group tests: Content score ANOVA F=24.44 (2, 797), p<.001, η2=.058 for GenAI experience; Age group F=3.92 (6, 793), p<.001, η2=.029; Education level F=9.28 (4, 791), p<.001, η2=.045; Gender t(792)=-3.271, p=.001. Nomological validity (SEM): analytic AI knowledge associations r=.244 to .447 depending on knowledge dimension; attitudes toward AI association with content knowledge r=.106, p=.026; trust in GenAI associations negative for overall/epistemic/society but not significant for content (reported as no significant associations for content). Additional analysis (Procedural AI knowledge score (0–9)): Known-group tests: Procedural score ANOVA F=38.03 (2, 441.7), p<.001, η2=.095 for GenAI experience (Welch); Age group F=3.53 (6, 785), p=.002, η2=.026; Education level F=19.39 (4, 363.8), p<.001, η2=.083; Gender t(796)=-1.621, p=.105 (not significant). Nomological validity (SEM): attitudes toward AI association with procedural knowledge r=.192, p<.001; trust in GenAI reported as no significant associations for content/procedural/technology-related/user-related dimensions. Additional analysis (Epistemic AI knowledge score (0–9)): Known-group tests: Epistemic score ANOVA F=34.04 (2, 797), p<.001, η2=.079 for GenAI experience; Age group F=4.09 (6, 793), p<.001, η2=.030; Education level F=21.19 (4, 793), p<.001, η2=.097; Gender t(796)=-2.556, p=.011. Nomological validity (SEM): trust in GenAI negative association with epistemic knowledge r=-.287, p<.001; attitudes toward AI no significant association with epistemic knowledge (reported as no significant associations for epistemic). Additional analysis (Technology-related AI knowledge score (0–9)): Known-group tests: Technology-related score ANOVA F=34.761 (2, 456), p<.001, η2=.084 for GenAI experience (Welch); Age group F=4.75 (6, 310.87), p<.001, η2=.040; Education level F=18.1 (4, 793), p<.001, η2=.084; Gender t(792)=-2.421, p=.016. Nomological validity (SEM): attitudes toward AI no significant association with technology-related knowledge; trust in GenAI no significant associations for technology-related dimension. Additional analysis (User-related AI knowledge score (0–12)): Known-group tests: User-related score ANOVA F=40.508 (2, 443.7), p<.001, η2=.098 for GenAI experience (Welch); Age group F=6.28 (6, 786), p<.001, η2=.046; Education level F=14.67 (4, 785), p<.001, η2=.070; Gender t(791)=-2.656, p=.008. Nomological validity (SEM): attitudes toward AI positive association with user-related knowledge r=.108, p=.041; trust in GenAI no significant associations for user-related dimension. Additional analysis (Society-related AI knowledge score (0–6)): Known-group tests: Society-related score ANOVA F=24.95 (2, 797), p<.001, η2=.050 for GenAI experience; Age group F=1.658 (6, 298.15), p=.124, η2=.012 (not significant); Education level F=16 (4, 795), p<.001, η2=.075; Gender t(796)=-1.927, p=.054 (not significant). Nomological validity (SEM): trust in GenAI negative association with society-related knowledge r=-.245, p<.001; attitudes toward AI no significant association with society-related knowledge.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the custom AI/GenAI knowledge inventory data from Israel’s adult internet users, the study leveraged accumulating GenAI experience, education level, gender, and age to explain variation in overall AI knowledge, finding that higher GenAI experience and higher education were associated with higher overall knowledge and that females and older/younger groups differed significantly by score. This indicates that AI knowledge measurement can detect meaningful demographic and experience-related gaps that can guide targeted adult AI education and training.

data.outcome_summary: This study developed and validated a performance-based two-axial AI/GenAI knowledge scale using an online quota-sampled survey of adult internet users in Israel (n=800; Oct–Nov 2024). The instrument measured overall AI knowledge (0–27) and sub-scores for knowledge types (content, procedural, epistemic) and knowledge domains (technology-related, user-related, society-related), using true/false/“I don’t know” items plus a separate analytic AI knowledge task. Psychometric validation relied on CFA (DWLS) and SEM with reported fit indices (e.g., overall SEM model CFI=.819, RMSEA=.06, SRMSR=.067) and known-group differences by GenAI experience, age, education, and gender (e.g., overall score GenAI experience F=47.24, p<.001, η2=.106). The study found that trust in GenAI was negatively associated with epistemic and society-related knowledge, while attitudes toward AI showed small positive associations with content/procedural/user-related knowledge. Limitations include the absence of documented survey-weight usage and missing-data handling, and the fact that the paper uses psychometric modeling rather than ML prediction.
